messages.subject: How to put code chunk into documentation as a literal?
messages.subject_clean: How to put code chunk into documentation as a literal?
messages.body_plain:
Hi, folks.  I've been trying to write up a document for a class that uses RStudio/knitr as the primary tool.  I wanted to show a prototypical code chunk in the document before actually launching into using code chunks.  I.e., I wanted to show:

        A typical code chunk looks like:

            ```{r}
                    (some R code goes here)
            ```

        Then blah, blah, blah, ...

I haven't been able to figure out how to do this.  I've tried using backslash escapes (\`) in various combinations.  I've tried embedding the whole thing in a ```...``` chunk.  I've tried combinations of that and escapes.  Basically I get either nothing at all in the knitted HTML document, or I get the text as I want it, except with the backslashes still visible  in the HTML.  Any suggestions?

Thanks,

-- Mike

I'm not quite sure what was the problem, but one major difference
between running knit() alone and compiling the vignettes using knitr
is that knitr will stop on errors in code chunks in the latter case,
and will not in the former case. That is because I set
opts_knit$set(stop_on_error = 2) before compiling package vignettes,
which can be helpful to prevent unexpected errors.

This is a decision that I find hard to make -- whether to stop on
error or not. By default, knitr does not stop, just like you paste the
code into R console, but this may not be a good choice because people
may not even notice the errors if knitr did not stop.

messages.body_plain:
As some of you may know, I have had a (rather late) mid-life crisis and run off with another language called Julia. (http://julialang.org)

It is a young language (release 0.2 is due out "real soon now").  Currently starting a julia process and loading various packages can be slow - on the order of a couple of seconds.  Writing a knitr language engine for Julia that started a new process for every chunk would probably be unacceptably slow at this point.  In addition it would be awkward to cache results for reuse in later chunks.

Has anyone experimented with a knitr language engine that execs a process and exchanges strings, say through a read-write pipe?

Right now I am using cut-and-paste from an ESS *julia* buffer in emacs into the .Rmd file but readers of this list know why that's not a good idea.

Thanks, but I do not have enough memory on my laptop (the object you
created requires about 8G memory). I will test this when I have access
to our servers. Before that, we can still figure out the root of this
problem. You can try this naive cache method via save() and load():

\documentclass{article}

\begin{document}

<<makeMatrix, cache=TRUE>>=

bigMatrix <- matrix(runif(1000000000), ncol = 1000)
print(object.size(bigMatrix), units = "Gb")

save(bigMatrix, file = 'bigMatrix.RData')
rm(bigMatrix)
@
<<loadMatrix, cache=FALSE>>=
load('bigMatrix.RData')
@

\end{document}

If this works, the problem came from lazyLoad(). Otherwise it is just
because R cannot load large objects under 64-bit Windows in certain
cases, as described in R 3.0.0 NEWS:

After slowly learning a tiny bit about Julia during the weekend, I
just succeeded with a prototype as illustrated here:
http://rpubs.com/yihui/julia-knitr

I first looked at the fifo (named pipe) approach, and it worked pretty
well, but it lacks portability, especially under Windows (I have no
idea how to create a fifo there). Then I experimented with socket
connections. It turns out to be usable, and I believe it is portable
to Windows as well.

I guess this might be a general solution to other languages, so I
packed what I have done into a small package:
https://github.com/yihui/runr

I still have a few questions, though:

1. The output is not really what we would have seen in Julia REPL,
e.g. [1:3] gives

3-element Int64 Array:
 1
 2
 3

but I can only get [1,2,3] because I'm using println() to capture the
output: https://github.com/yihui/runr/blob/master/inst/lang/julia_socket.jl
I do not know how to faithfully reproduce the console output. A
related question is here: http://stackoverflow.com/q/17769065/559676
In particular, the side effects of print()/println() in the code will
be lost (no way to redirect stdout at the moment).

2. I have not used "try catch" yet; when the Julia code is
problematic, the process will be terminated.

3. I do not know how to find a usable TCP port in R. The default 2000
may not always be available.

4. I do not understand scopes yet, so the code might be evaluated in
the wrong environment. (what are globalenv() and parent.frame() in
Julia?)

There might be other problems. Please feel free to improve this
package. Eventually knitr will depend on it.

The Rmd source for that Rpubs post is:

# Run Julia from R

First we set up the Julia engine.

```{r setup}
library(knitr)
library(runr)
j = proc_julia()
j$start()
knit_engines$set(julia = function(options) {
  knitr:::wrap(j$exec(options$code), options)
})
```

Test a sequence of numbers:

```{r test-a, engine='julia'}
a = [1:10]
a + 9
```

Test a function:

```{r test-b, engine='julia'}
b(x) = x^2 + 2x + 1
b(5)
x = {"a", "b", "c"}
```

Do not forget to shut it down in the end.

```{r quit}
j$stop()
```

Duncan's email confirmed my guess. Now I do not think it is possible
to solve the problem (I might be wrong). While the evaluate package
tries to emulate the R console, there are still some edge cases that
it cannot cover.

I'm not sure if I can explain this clearly to you. Maybe you can
ignore knitr at the moment, and imagine the knitr function is
capture.output() (while in fact it is knit(), but that is not
important). Now you see how capture.output() fails to capture the
output:

> times <- function(total = 3, name="a") {

+     ctr <- 1
+     function(expr, val, ok, visible) {
+         cat("[Task ", name, "] ", ctr,"\n", sep="")
+         ctr <<- ctr + 1
+         return(ctr <= total)
+     }
+ }

>
> h <- taskCallbackManager()
> h$suspend()
> h$add(times())

[1] "1"
> h$add(times(4,"b"))
[1] "2"
> h$add(times(5,"c"))
[1] "3"
> h$add(times(6,"d"))
[1] "4"

> capture.output(h$suspend(FALSE))
character(0)

[Task a] 1
[Task b] 1
[Task c] 1
[Task d] 1

> capture.output(print(1:5))
[1] "[1] 1 2 3 4 5"

See the second command has captured the output, but the first one has
not: it is an empty character vector. The reason that the output
escaped capture.output() is the output from your callback function
comes _after_ the top-level command returns, i.e. after
capture.output() has returned the value, the callback function is
executed.

That is exactly the same reason why you cannot see the output from
knit(). There is an inherent dilemma: the output happens after your
function call, so you cannot write a function to capture the output.
You may think, well, let me write another function to capture the
output of this function, but then that "another function" becomes the
top-level command, and the output happens after that function. You
just can never reach it.

This is really a deep corner of R. I guess knitr cannot help much here.

Regards,
Yihui
